newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada limiting use of replacing striking workers.
newsitem.headline: Canada limiting use of replacing striking workers.

text.p: Canadian Labor Minister Alfonso Gagliano introduced legislation on Monday that would restrict some employers' ability to hire replacement workers during a strike but would protect Canada's important grain exports.
"The amendments to ... the Canada Labor Code are important, timely and essential, but they are not radical," Gagliano told a news conference.
The bill would only apply to federal employees and to companies regulated by the federal government such as banks, airlines, broadcasters and ports.

It did not introduce a general prohibition on the use of replacement workers, sometimes called "scabs" by unions, but it did say that if the employers use replacement workers "for the purpose of undermining a union's representative capacity," a newly established Canada Labor Relations Board could rule this an unfair labor practice.

Al Gidaro, legislative assistant to Gagliano, explained that a company would not, for example, be allowed to reach an agreement with a union and then turn around and say it would continue to use its replacement workers.
The legislation would give added protection to grain exports.

"The shipment of grain is a multi-million dollar industry. We export to over 70 countries and the livelihood of over 130,000 farmers depends on our reputation as a reliable supplier and exporter," Gagliano said.
Grain handlers and their employers would retain the right to strike and lock out -- and shut down grain shipments.
"In the event of a work stoppage involving other parties in port-related activities, including longshoremen, services affecting grain shipment must be maintained," Gagliano said.
The effectiveness of the measures would be reviewed in 1999 and if necessary Ottawa would examine stronger measures.

Since 1972, a dozen strikes have affected Canadian grain shipments, Gidaro said. Nine involved longshoremen -- who will now have to maintain service to grain vessels -- while only three involved grain handlers.
Gagliano said he hoped to push the bill through Parliament by spring.
